messages.subject: batch processing using apply and/or dplyr and seq()
messages.subject_clean: batch processing using apply and/or dplyr and seq()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a data frame with individual id "Band" and dates/times "DateTime" in POSIXct format. I want to create a regularized time interval of 150 seconds between DateTimes, starting with the first DateTime within each individual and ending with the final time. (If you think I'm heading towards interpolation, you'd be correct!) However, batch processing this is getting to be a big PITA.

If I subset the df by individual ID "bird553", using seq() works:

ti <- seq(bird553$DateTime[1], bird553$DateTime[length(bird553$DateTime)],
          by = 150)

Here are my attempts to batch process:

ti <- all %>%
  group_by(Band) %>%
  mutate(seq(all$DateTime[1], all$DateTime[length(all$DateTime)],
      by = 150))
Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) :
  Column `seq(all$date[1], all$date[length(all$date)], by = 158)` must be length 2538 (the group size) or one, not 205888

ti <- tapply(all$DateTime, all$Band, seq(all$date[1], all$date[length(all$date)], by = 150))
Error in match.fun(FUN) : 'seq(all$date[1], all$date[length(all$date)], by = 150)' is not a function, character or symbol

I've done different variations on the code above, but essentially I don't think I'm calling to the correct elements in the df. I'd like to figure out how to loop this code through subsets of individual IDs of the df. I know generally this might be easier using adehabitatLT, but for the moment I don't want to convert LL to UTMs. Thanks all!

Corey

As Brandon said, an example dataset would definitely help for testing. But upon quick glance, I think there's another issue with how you're trying to use 'group_by()'. If I understand your problem correctly, you want a DateTime sequence for every individual bird ID (each "Band"), but this sequence may be of variable length for each bird. However, dplyr is meant to work naturally with dataframes, and when you use 'group_by()' in this case, dplyr is expecting to return a dataframe with a number of rows equal to the number of individual birds in the dataset (since you grouped by "Band"). When you then use 'mutate()' to create your new variable, dplyr is expecting to return only one value for each bird, yet what you actually want is a sequence of values for each bird. Your variable referencing issues aside (i.e., the $ stuff Brandon brought up), you're attempting to ask dplyr to squeeze what you successfully generated using your 'seq()' implementation into one cell of a dataframe. And it's putting up a fuss. I think you're going to need to either switch to recording your sequences for each bird in a list or generate a dataframe such that you have a column for 1) "Band", 2) the DateTime sequence element number (ranging from 1 to whatever the sequence length should be for each bird), and 3) the DateTime sequence values themselves. Using this second strategy, your dataframe is going to be much longer than whatever your number of birds is and there will be a variable number of entries for each individual "Band", as I believe you want.

Hope that helps!
Evan

This is the where we enter the tidyverse’s diabolical world of nested data frames through tidyr:
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

#Make fake data, birds where each one has a time sequence of randomly
#spaced times
the_birds <- data_frame(Band = rep(1:10, each = sample.int <http://sample.int>(20, 1, TRUE))) %>%
  group_by(Band) %>%
  mutate(DateTime = Sys.time() + cumsum(sample.int <http://sample.int>(200, n(), TRUE))) %>%
  group_by()

# Make a regularly-spaced sequence for each bird
# Since mutate() expects an object the same length of the birds, and
# summarise() wants objects of length one, we return length-1 sequnces by
# turning them into a list-column, then expanding it with unnest()
regular_birds <- the_birds %>%
  group_by(Band) %>%
  summarise(TimeSeq = list(seq(min(DateTime), max(DateTime), by = 150))) %>%
  unnest(TimeSeq)

# To do this while escaping the tidyprisonwithnowalls, you can split the data
# by bird and lapply across each data frame to generate sequences
base_regular_birds <-
  do.call(rbind,
          lapply(
            split(the_birds, the_birds$Band), function(x) {
              data.frame(Band = x$Band[1],
                         TimeSeq = seq(min(x$DateTime), max(x$DateTime), by = 150))
            })
  )

# For sake of testing. base stuff messes around with rownames, tidyverse adds
# additional tibbly classes.
rownames(base_regular_birds) <- NULL
identical(base_regular_birds, as.data.frame(regular_birds)) # TRUE

I'm certain you can do something like that. Below is some ***very*** old code of mine (mostly borrowed from SO posts) that does a correlation matrix. With geom_tile you can do the fill as your "heat" and then use geom_text to place your groupings.

Hopefully you can see how to apply something like this to your situation?

#Correlation matrix plot
library(tidyverse)
raw.data <- mtcars
colstart = 1
colend = length(names(raw.data))

c<-cor(raw.data[colstart:colend], use= "pairwise.complete.obs")

#Correlation p-value tests
cor.pvalues <- function(X){

    nc <- ncol(X)
    res <- matrix(0, nc, nc)
    for (i in 2:nc){
        for (j in 1:(i - 1)){
            res[i, j] <- res[j, i] <- cor.test(X[,i], X[,j])$p.value
            }
        }
    res
    }

p <- cor.pvalues(raw.data[colstart:colend])

#convert p-values into stars for significance level
stars <- as.character(symnum(p, cutpoints=c(0,0.001,0.01,0.05,1),
                      symbols=c('***', '**', '*', '' ),
                      legend=FALSE,
                      ))

#Combine into data.frame for plotting
molten.p <- reshape2::melt(p)
molten.c <- reshape2::melt(c)
molten.stars <- reshape2::melt(stars)
molten.raw.data <- bind_cols(molten.c, molten.p[3], molten.stars[1])

#rename columns to avoid the same name
names(molten.raw.data) <- c("M1", "M2", "corr", "pvalue", "stars")

#define each triangle of the plot matric and the diagonal (mi.ids)
mi.ids <- subset(molten.raw.data, M1 == M2)
mi.lower <- subset(molten.raw.data[lower.tri(c),], M1 != M2)
mi.upper <- subset(molten.raw.data[upper.tri(c),], M1 != M2)
stars.lower <- subset(molten.raw.data[lower.tri(c),], M1 != M2)
meas <- as.character(unique(molten.raw.data$M2))

ggplot(molten.raw.data, aes(M1, M2, fill=corr))+
theme_bw()+
geom_tile(data=mi.lower) +
geom_text(data=mi.lower, aes(label=paste(stars)), size=1) +
geom_text(data=mi.ids, aes(label=M2), hjust=0, colour="grey40", size=1)+
scale_colour_identity() +
scale_fill_gradientn(colours= c("darkblue", "lightblue", "white", "pink", "darkred")) +
scale_x_discrete("", limits=meas[length(meas):1]) + #flip the x axis
scale_y_discrete("", limits=meas)+
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90, hjust=1, vjust=0.5))+
guides(fill=F, colour=F)

Again, super old code, but just for an idea.

B

Dear D-RUGgies,

I am interested in using R to calculate some landscape metrics, similar to what I've used fragstats to do in the past (some examples of such metrics are here:
http://www.umass.edu/landeco/teaching/landscape_ecology/schedule/chapter9_metrics.pdf). The landscapes of interests are circular buffers around my study sites.

I know there are a few R packages that can potentially do this. Some seem to be limited to binary landscapes (only two cover classes), though, and I am working with landscapes with multiple cover classes (and I want to use metrics that involve >2 cover classes, like interspersion).

Also, some packages seem to require the landscape data be in a text-based raster, or at least some kind of raster. I can convert to raster if necessary (although I'm not sure how to convert to a text raster), but my landscape cover data is in polygons right now, and I'm wondering if there's any way to analyze it without converting it.

Not sure if this is possible exactly as described, so I'd appreciate any suggestions for reasonable ways to go about it! I'm open to other approaches besides R too. Fragstats seemed pretty clunky last time I used it so I'm hoping to avoid it if possible.

Thanks much,
Jesse

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’ve found solve(), which I’m using millions of times, to be extremely slow on FARM. Specifically, the example below takes ~0.2 seconds both on my mobile-core ultrabook and when I run in on an entire node on FARM (eg, using srun –p high –N 1 –c 24 –t 1:00:00 --pty  -R). Running it on anything less than a full node on FARM (eg, srun –p high –N 1 –c 22 –t 1:00:00 --pty  -R), however, takes 20sec (100x slower). Bill Broadley suggested it might be because R assumes/acts like its getting all 24 cores/threads on the node when in fact it has access to fewer cores.

1 – If this makes sense (I’m skeptical because I’ve never seen this issue before with other commands that make use of parallelization), is there a way to limit R to use a specific number of cores within a running R session?

2 – Are there good alternatives to solve() that might not run into this issue? I know chol2inv(chol(A)) is one option, but unfortunately its not suited to the matrices I’m working with.

Many thanks!!

Vadim

Example:

start=proc.time();  set.seed(1); A=matrix(rnorm(45^2),45,45);

for(i in 1:1e2) solve(A);  end=proc.time(); end-start;

messages.body_plain:
Hi D-RUGies,

I am trying to figure out if it's possible to efficiently use a data frame of parameter values as inputs to a function that runs a population model.  Ideally, the solution would use tidyverse functions.  I was trying to use the function map() across a list of nested data frames, but it's clear that R can't figure out that the variables are located within each data frame (see the error below in red).  I'd like to get the value of N.fished out of the population model function, and have it attached to each nested data set somewhere.

Attached is the data RF_parms.  Here is the code:

library(tidyverse)
library(purrrlyr)
library(purrr)

RF_parms <- read.csv("~/RFparmsforMEGAFUNCTION_LY.csv")
RF_parms.list <- RF_parms %>%
    group_by(Species) %>%
    nest()

#1. Function to model population
openpop_time = function(df) {
  df %>%
  a_harv0=(log((Lfish-Linf)/-Linf)/-k)+a0
  agefish=round(a_harv0,digits=0)
  N0=rep(100,maxage)
  N0[1]=R
  s=exp(-M)
  sf=exp(-(M+Fi))
  sfx=rep(sf,maxage-1)
  sfx[1:(agefish-1)]=rep(s,(agefish-1))
  sxs=rep(s,maxage-1)
  Nt = matrix(0,tf,maxage)
  Nt[1,] = N0
  t<-1

  for(t in 1:(tf-1)) {
    Nt[t+1,1] = R
    Nt[t+1,2:(maxage)] = sfx*Nt[t,1:(maxage-1)]
  }

  N.fished=Nt[tf,]
  return(N.fished)
}

RF_parms.list2 <- RF_parms.list %>% mutate(N.fished = map(data, openpop_time))

Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) :
  Evaluation error: object 'a0' not found.

Any insight would be greatly appreciated!  Thanks for your time.

Lauren

That said, I've seen pmap used in many examples for this sort of thing. Perhaps that would be better used here? Hard to say since I don't fully see what you want your function to do.

HTH,
B

 saveRDS(res, file=paste('C:/mypath/test_pred_all", chunk, ".rds'))

- you return(new, end) looks suspicious: you can only return a single object, possibly a list though
-I don;t think you necessarily need a function(chunk) in your code?

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
arg <- commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)
chunk<-arg[1]
print(chunk)

set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(1:100)

res <- x[as.numeric(chunk)]
saveRDS(res, file = paste("result_", chunk, '.rds', sep=""))

You may consider additional measures to make the code more memory-safe. E.g. there is no need to find the all rows with NA for each chunk ( i <- which(!is.na <http://is.na/>(all_df_0624_1201$NDVI_0624)) ). You can find the rows with NA within each chunk, predict the cases without NA and keep the predicted values as NA for input with NA. In this way you will have equal number of rows between input and predictions, which will make it lot easier to create the raster of prediction (assuming that is your final goal). Your final myscript.R should look like:

arg<-commandArgs()

fun(chunk){
  end<-chunk*1000000
  start<-end-1000000-1

  indf <-  all_df_0624_1201[start:end,]
  i <-   which(!is.na <http://is.na/>(indf$NDVI_0624))
  # now create an empty vector to store the results
  prediction <- rep(NA, nrow(indf))
  prediction[i] <- predict(svm_05082018_Radial_Landsatlike, newdata = indf[i,])
  outfile <- paste0(' C:/mypath/ ','test_pred_all',chuck,'.rds') # set the output name for each chunk
  saveRDS( prediction, file = outfile)
  return(c(start,end, nrow(indf), length(prediction))
  }

messages.subject: Dealing with imbalanced presence/absence data
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with imbalanced presence/absence data
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm doing some species distribution modeling (MaxEnt via 'dismo') with a presence/absence data set with very unbalanced classes. I have 76 presence points and 2949 absence points. Using all of the data, I get very low positive predictive value (percent of all positives which are true positives), around 10%. I tried the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE, via 'DMwR') with similar results. I've also tried undersampling, which seems to go much better, but based on my reading, it is not as reliable/accurate as SMOTE. Any recommendations? I realize that it could be this dataset is just not going to be very predictive. However, I would like to rule out other possibilities before coming to that conclusion.

Cheers,
Elise Hellwig
